set.explanation: Pneumonia is defined as symptoms of lower respiratory tract infection with new radiographic shadowing, so the chest X-ray confirms the diagnosis and shows its extent, cavitation or effusion. Blood and sputum cultures identify the organism in only a minority of cases, a raised white cell count and CRP are non-specific markers of infection, and arterial blood gases assess severity (respiratory failure) rather than the diagnosis. In primary care NICE allows a clinical diagnosis with CRP guidance, but a hospital diagnosis needs a chest X-ray.

why: Same idea as resinf-0021 (chronic fever and haemoptysis in a young adult from a high-prevalence setting = M. tuberculosis)

set.stem: A man has recently been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Which cells engulf the inhaled bacilli and go on to form the granulomatous lesions?
set.explanation: Inhaled M. tuberculosis is ingested by alveolar macrophages, in which it survives by blocking phagosome–lysosome fusion. CD4 T cells then release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages; these transform into epithelioid cells and fuse into Langhans giant cells to wall off the infection as a granuloma. Epithelioid and giant cells are therefore derived from macrophages, T lymphocytes orchestrate rather than engulf, and neutrophils play little part in the granuloma.

why: Same idea as resinf-0001 (suspected pulmonary TB with upper-zone shadowing: sputum AFB is the confirmatory test)

set.stem: A middle-aged man is diagnosed with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis. He has no known drug allergies. Which drug is least likely to be included in his initial treatment?
set.explanation: Standard treatment (WHO and NICE) for drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis is 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid, given with pyridoxine and ideally with directly observed or video-observed therapy. Streptomycin is an injectable aminoglycoside with ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity and is no longer part of first-line regimens; it is reserved for selected resistant cases.

Rifampicin colours urine, sweat and tears orange-red (it can stain soft contact lenses), which is harmless but should be explained before treatment starts. It is also a potent hepatic enzyme inducer that reduces the effect of the combined contraceptive pill, warfarin, corticosteroids and many antiretrovirals. Isoniazid causes neuropathy and hepatitis, ethambutol optic neuritis, pyrazinamide hepatitis and gout, and streptomycin ototoxicity.

why: Same idea as resinf-0063 (hotel-linked pneumonia with confusion and GI symptoms = Legionella)

set.stem: A 50-year-old man with long-standing COPD develops insidious aching in the distal limbs, particularly both wrists, and has lost 4.5 kg (10 lb). The skin over the wrists is warm and red, and there is bilateral finger clubbing. Plain X-rays of the wrists show periosteal thickening, reported as possible osteomyelitis. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: Clubbing with painful symmetrical periostitis of the distal long bones is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy, most often caused by lung cancer (especially non-small cell) and less often by chronic suppurative lung disease; COPD itself does not cause clubbing, so a chest X-ray (then CT) is the next step. Bilateral symmetrical periosteal reaction is not osteomyelitis, so antibiotics and joint aspiration are unhelpful, methotrexate treats rheumatoid arthritis, and an ESR would not change management. HPOA often improves after the tumour is resected.

why: Parse fragment (first half of a split question, no options); its content is merged into resinf-0107

set.stem: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency department with haemoptysis. He has antiphospholipid syndrome and takes warfarin. Chest auscultation is normal, but there is nasal crusting and reduced sensation to both ankles. The chest X-ray shows cavitating nodules in both mid-zones. Hb 138 g/L, urea 15.6 mmol/L, creatinine 240 µmol/L, CRP 145 mg/L, INR 1.4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Nasal crusting, cavitating lung nodules, acute kidney injury and a peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) form the ENT–lung–kidney pattern of granulomatosis with polyangiitis; check PR3-ANCA and urine for blood and casts. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA) causes nephritis and alveolar haemorrhage without granulomatous nasal disease or cavitating nodules, anti-GBM disease has no ENT or neurological involvement, and the subtherapeutic INR and nodules argue against pulmonary embolism. Staphylococcal septic emboli would not explain the nasal crusting and neuropathy.

why: Two parse fragments merged into one self-contained question; source had no key (set to granulomatosis with polyangiitis)
Same idea as ild-0011 (RA on methotrexate with obstructive spirometry = bronchiolitis obliterans); source key (methotrexate pneumonitis) was also wrong

set.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a dry cough, progressive breathlessness and recurrent chest infections. His GP recently started a salbutamol inhaler, with little effect. There is diffuse wheeze. Investigations show blood eosinophilia and total IgE 2300 kU/L, and the chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. What is the treatment of choice?
set.explanation: Asthma-like symptoms with eosinophilia, a total IgE above 1000 kU/L and pulmonary infiltrates indicate allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus colonising the airways. Oral glucocorticoids (prednisolone, tapered over months) are first-line, and itraconazole is an alternative or steroid-sparing agent; IgE levels guide response. Low-dose ICS alone does not control the infiltrates, nebulised antibiotics are for Pseudomonas in bronchiectasis, and IVIG and rituximab have no role.

set.stem: A middle-aged woman has progressive breathlessness. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Calcium 2.7 mmol/L; angiotensin-converting enzyme 200 µg/L (normal below 40). Given the likely diagnosis, which feature is associated with a good prognosis?
set.explanation: Sarcoidosis presenting acutely with erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (Löfgren syndrome) has the best prognosis, with spontaneous remission in most patients within 2 years. Poor prognostic features include lupus pernio, insidious onset, age over 40, black ethnicity, hypercalcaemia, extrapulmonary disease (cardiac, neurological, renal) and parenchymal fibrosis on imaging.

Loss of consciousness during a seizure allows aspiration of oropharyngeal flora, and days later foul-smelling (putrid) sputum indicates anaerobic infection (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, anaerobic streptococci), which may progress to lung abscess or empyema. Treatment should include anaerobic cover (e.g. co-amoxiclav, or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole). Chemical pneumonitis appears within hours of gastric aspiration and does not produce foul sputum a week later, and Mycoplasma, Gram-negative and Gram-positive aerobes do not explain putrid sputum.

set.stem: A 47-year-old homeless man with alcohol misuse is admitted with increasing breathlessness, sweats and purulent sputum. A few days ago he was brought to the emergency department unconscious but self-discharged when he woke. He is febrile, with dullness and bronchial breathing in the right mid-zone, and the chest X-ray shows right middle-lobe consolidation. What is the most likely cause?
set.explanation: Recent loss of consciousness from alcohol is the key risk: depressed cough and gag reflexes allow aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions, producing pneumonia a few days later in a dependent segment (right lung, lower or middle lobe), so antibiotics with anaerobic cover are needed. Tuberculosis is a consideration in a homeless drinker but causes weeks of illness with upper-lobe disease, and Chlamydia, Legionella and Mycoplasma do not explain the link to the unconscious episode.

why: Source key (tuberculosis) did not fit an acute illness days after an unconscious episode with middle-lobe consolidation; key changed to aspiration and the contradictory 'dullness at the apex' corrected

set.stem: An 81-year-old woman who saw her GP with influenza-like symptoms 2 weeks ago now presents with increasing cough, purulent sputum and haemoptysis, and has become acutely confused. She is agitated with a respiratory rate of 35/min and is hypoxic; WBC 20 × 10⁹/L (mainly neutrophils), creatinine 250 µmol/L. The chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation with necrosis and empyema. What diagnosis best fits this picture?
set.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza; it is necrotising, producing patchy consolidation with cavities, pneumatocoeles, abscesses and empyema, severe sepsis and a high mortality, and Panton–Valentine leukocidin-producing strains can kill young patients within days. BTS guidance is to add flucloxacillin (or vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA is possible) to the usual high-severity regimen. Pneumococcal pneumonia is also common after influenza but rarely causes necrosis and cavitation; Haemophilus, Mycoplasma and psittacosis do not cause this necrotising picture.

why: Source key (Streptococcus pneumoniae) was wrong: post-influenza necrotising pneumonia with empyema is Staphylococcus aureus

set.explanation: Long-standing productive cough, halitosis, haemoptysis and inspiratory crackles indicate bronchiectasis, and BTS guidance puts airway clearance by chest physiotherapy (postural drainage, active cycle of breathing, oscillating PEP devices), taught by a respiratory physiotherapist and done daily, at the core of reducing sputum retention and exacerbations. For patients with 3 or more exacerbations a year, long-term macrolide (azithromycin) or inhaled antibiotics are added. Rotating cyclical antibiotics are not recommended, inhaled corticosteroids are only for coexisting asthma, bronchodilators do not reduce exacerbations, and surgery is reserved for localised refractory disease.

set.stem: A 26-year-old office secretary who smokes 10–15 cigarettes a day presents with a couple of episodes of haemoptysis. She has felt tired recently and has passed cola-coloured urine. A full blood count shows anaemia and the chest X-ray shows blotchy shadowing over both lung fields. She is ANCA-negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Haemoptysis with bilateral alveolar shadowing, anaemia from blood loss into the lungs and nephritic cola-coloured urine is a pulmonary–renal syndrome; with negative ANCA, anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease is most likely, and smoking predisposes to the pulmonary haemorrhage. Anti-GBM antibodies and renal biopsy with linear IgG staining confirm it, and treatment is plasma exchange with steroids and cyclophosphamide. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is usually ANCA-positive with ENT involvement, and carcinoma, tuberculosis and sarcoidosis do not cause acute glomerulonephritis.

set.stem: A 25-year-old man with epilepsy aspirated gastric contents during a seizure (Mendelson syndrome). What is the most likely clinical sign?
set.explanation: Aspiration of acidic gastric juice causes a chemical pneumonitis within hours, with bronchospasm (wheeze), tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxaemia and patchy infiltrates, sometimes progressing to ARDS. Management is supportive (suction, oxygen, bronchodilators, ventilation if needed), and antibiotics are added only if infection develops. Tachypnoea rather than bradypnoea is expected, laryngospasm protects against aspiration, and paradoxical breathing and percussion tenderness are not features.

set.stem: A 35-year-old woman being treated for asthma has worsening cough and wheeze with recurrent fleeting pulmonary infiltrates. She coughs up brownish plugs, and her chest X-ray shows pulmonary infiltration with some lobar consolidation. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
set.explanation: Poorly controlled asthma with brown mucus plugs (containing fungal hyphae) and transient, migratory infiltrates is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a type I and III hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways; tests show eosinophilia, total IgE above 1000 kU/L, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG and later central bronchiectasis. Aspergilloma is a fungal ball in an existing cavity, simple asthma does not cause fleeting infiltrates, and bronchiectasis and tuberculosis do not explain the plugs and migrating shadows.

set.stem: A 22-year-old student attends clinic 6 weeks after admission with pneumonia. Which of the following complications of pneumonia is a chronic rather than an acute complication of the infection?
set.explanation: Severe or necrotising pneumonia, especially in childhood (measles, pertussis) or with tuberculosis, can permanently damage the bronchial walls, leaving bronchiectasis as a chronic structural sequela. Empyema, lung abscess and bronchopleural fistula are acute or subacute complications arising during or shortly after the infection, and post-infective organising pneumonia is a subacute, usually steroid-responsive process. A follow-up chest X-ray at about 6 weeks is advised for persisting symptoms or high cancer risk.

why: Source key (organising pneumonia) replaced by bronchiectasis, the classic chronic sequela; the source's own stray explanation for this item gives bronchiectasis

set.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae spreads in closed communities such as barracks, schools and colleges, affects young adults and causes a gradual atypical pneumonia in which the chest X-ray often looks worse than the chest examination. Cold agglutinins (IgM against the I antigen on red cells) are present in about half of cases and may cause haemolysis; diagnosis is by PCR or serology and treatment is a macrolide or doxycycline. Klebsiella affects alcohol users, Legionella has travel and water-system links, Q fever follows animal exposure, and viral pneumonia does not produce cold agglutinins.

Chronic purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections and coarse basal crackles indicate bronchiectasis, which is more common in rheumatoid arthritis (particularly in seropositive disease) and carries a worse prognosis; HRCT confirms it. RA-associated interstitial fibrosis gives a dry cough with fine end-inspiratory crackles, chronic bronchitis requires smoking, and carcinoma and tuberculosis would cause weight loss or haemoptysis rather than years of recurrent purulent infections.

set.stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with suspected pneumonia. Temperature 38.3°C, respiratory rate 27/min, BP 100/70 mmHg, and she is confused. Serum urea is 5.2 mmol/L. According to the CURB-65 criteria, which of these findings is associated with a worse prognosis?
set.explanation: Only her new confusion meets a CURB-65 criterion. The thresholds are urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate 30/min or more, systolic BP below 90 mmHg or diastolic 60 mmHg or less, and age 65 or over, so her urea of 5.2, respiratory rate of 27, BP of 100/70 and age of 62 all score zero. A score of 1 is low severity, but confusion should always prompt a check for hypoxia and sepsis, and clinical judgement can override the score.

The mainstay of treatment for extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) is identifying and avoiding the antigen; corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg, tapered) speed recovery in acute severe or progressive disease, with mycophenolate or azathioprine as steroid-sparing agents and antifibrotics for progressive fibrosis. It is an immune-mediated (type III/IV) reaction, not an infection, so antibiotics are useless, desensitisation and immunoglobulins have no role, and NSAIDs do not alter the lung inflammation.

why: Source key (NSAIDs) is wrong; corticosteroids are the treatment besides antigen avoidance

set.stem: Which one of the following does NOT increase the risk of death in a patient with severe pneumonia?
options: Atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response
set.explanation: Age counts against the patient only at 65 years or more in CURB-65, so being 49 does not add risk. Low diastolic BP (60 mmHg or less) and urea above 7 mmol/L are CURB-65 criteria, while leucopenia (below 4 × 10⁹/L) and new arrhythmia such as fast atrial fibrillation are recognised additional adverse features, reflecting overwhelming sepsis and cardiac stress respectively. Other poor prognostic markers include hypoxaemia, multilobar involvement and coexisting disease.

set.stem: A 48-year-old man who has kept parrots for many years has had slowly progressive breathlessness and a dry cough for 2 years. There are fine crackles in the upper and mid zones. You suspect chronic extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) due to parrot antigen. Which finding would be most consistent with this diagnosis?
set.explanation: Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis from continuing antigen exposure produces fibrosis that is characteristically upper and mid-zone predominant, with a restrictive defect and reduced gas transfer; avian precipitins (IgG) and lavage lymphocytosis support the diagnosis. Positive Chlamydia antibodies indicate psittacosis, a bird-acquired infection rather than an allergic alveolitis; a raised IgE reflects type I atopy, as in asthma or ABPA; and the typical lung-function pattern is restrictive, not obstructive.

why: Truncated stem ('He c...and regular') rebuilt to stand alone, with the misleading wheeze removed; key unchanged

set.stem: A 32-year-old man sees his GP with cough and fever, and tuberculosis is suspected. He comes from an area with high rates of drug resistance. Which blood test is most important before starting treatment?
set.explanation: Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are all hepatotoxic, so baseline liver function tests are essential to identify pre-existing liver disease and to interpret later rises; NICE also advises renal function, FBC, HIV, hepatitis B and C serology and baseline visual acuity and colour vision for ethambutol. In an area of high drug resistance, sputum must also go for rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance. Clotting, platelets, haemoglobin and calcium are not specifically needed before first-line therapy.
